Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on what I have done wrong
I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
I can't deal with even the slightest upset
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' Those two states can sometimes fluctuate, but as selected core items they describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are not clinically coherent without further qualification.

issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: The trigger set is weakly tied to the rest of the profile and to an assault trauma. 'Object Throwing' fits a violence/attack context, but 'Expressions of Affection' and 'Children Present' imply very different cue meanings that are not supported by the threat, memory, or appraisal items. There is no corresponding interpersonal/sexual-contact theme, child-related meaning, or caregiving theme elsewhere in the profile, making these triggers hard to reconcile as part of the same assault-related presentation.

As a maladaptive strategy it does not align well with the active links from triggers/threat/negative appraisals in this formulation.

vignette: Kofi had always been drawn to the fast-paced world of urban planning, but after the assault six months ago, every crowded street and chaotic construction site seemed to hold a new menace. The smell of alcohol, which used to remind him of college parties, now transported him back to that night. Even the sound of objects being thrown or people expressing anger calmly made his heart rate spike. These triggers had become ubiquitous in his daily life as an urban planner, and Kofi found himself avoiding certain projects or meetings, fearing he might be confronted with one of these stimuli. As a result, Kofi began to ruminate on what he could have done differently that night, dwelling on self-blame. He became convinced that if only he had been more assertive or vigilant, the assault wouldn't have happened. This self-doubt seeped into other areas of his life, making him question his ability to cope with even minor setbacks. He started to feel helpless, as if bad things were bound to happen to him no matter what he did. Kofi's colleagues noticed a change in him; he became more withdrawn and hesitant to take on new challenges. To distract himself from these feelings of inadequacy, Kofi turned to gambling. He would spend hours online, trying to win back the sense of control he felt he had lost. But even as he gambled, he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was in danger. Every sudden sound or movement made him jump, and he found himself constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats. Kofi's memories of the assault were fragmented, consisting of vivid snapshots: the sound of shattering glass, the feel of pavement beneath his face, and the smell of alcohol wafting through the air. When these memories resurfaced, Kofi felt overwhelmed by emotion, unable to articulate what had happened. He would try to describe the events to friends or family, but the words got stuck in his throat. As he struggled to make sense of his experiences, Kofi began to feel that the people and institutions that were supposed to protect him had failed. The police hadn't taken his report seriously, and the hospital staff seemed more concerned with paperwork than his well-being. This perceived institutional failure reinforced his feelings of helplessness and low coping ability. Kofi's negative appraisals fed back into his maladaptive strategies; he became even more withdrawn, avoiding conflicts or situations that might trigger another episode of anxiety. His self-blame rumination intensified, making him wonder if he was somehow to blame for the assault. As a result, Kofi started to doubt his own perceptions of safety, constantly second-guessing whether he was truly secure. As the months went by, Kofi's avoidance behaviors took a toll on his relationships and work performance. His colleagues noticed that he was no longer contributing to team meetings, and his girlfriend eventually broke up with him due to his increasing withdrawal. It was only when Kofi realized that he had lost all sense of control over his life that he finally sought help. He hoped therapy could help him break the cycle of self-doubt and fear, but what frightened him most was the prospect of reliving those traumatic memories once again.
